name: Tool2Vec + ToolRefiner (Efficient and Scalable Estimation of Tool Representations in Vector Space)
venue: arXiv preprint (arXiv:2409.02141, cs.LG; submitted 2 Sep 2024, v1). No peer-reviewed venue found; the official BibTeX is @misc{moon2024efficient,...,archivePrefix={arXiv}}, indicating an arXiv-only release as of verification.
authors_affiliation: Suhong Moon* (UC Berkeley), Siddharth Jha* (UC Berkeley), Lutfi Eren Erdogan (UC Berkeley), Sehoon Kim (UC Berkeley), Woosang Lim (POSCO HOLDINGS), Kurt Keutzer (UC Berkeley), Amir Gholami (UC Berkeley / Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, LBNL). *Equal contribution. Primary affiliation: UC Berkeley (SqueezeAILab); with POSCO HOLDINGS and LBNL.
task_domain: tool-use / function calling for LLMs; specifically the tool (API) retrieval subproblem - selecting the minimal relevant set of tools to place in an LLM's context for downstream function calling.
problem_setting: Offline, non-interactive multi-tool retrieval. Given a natural-language user query and a large tool/API library (hundreds-to-thousands of tools), efficiently retrieve the relevant subset of tools so that only their descriptions/signatures are placed in the LLM prompt (addressing context-window/latency/cost limits). Single-agent, retrieval-as-front-end setting; supervision is available because domain-specific (query, tool-set) labels are synthesized by LLMs. The paper motivates that LLM-based retrieval (e.g. AnyTool) incurs seconds of latency and fine-tuning LLMs needs frequent retraining, so it instead trains small encoder models (E5-base; DeBERTa-V3 base/xsmall). The setting is multi-label: each query maps to 1-to-several required tools (up to 5 in ToolBank). Retrieval is decoupled from execution; the work does not run the downstream LLM tool-calling, only measures retrieval quality.
what_is_retrieved: tools (specifically tool/API entries from a tool library). Each retrieved tool is represented by a usage-driven embedding (Tool2Vec) or a classification logit (MLC); the downstream consumer would place the retrieved tool descriptions/signatures into the LLM context.
retrieval_grounding: STATIC external corpus: a fixed tool/API library (ToolBench RapidAPI hierarchy; or ToolBank's NumPy/Pandas/Boto3 tool sets). The retrievable store (Tool2Vec embeddings / MLC tool labels) is induced offline from training data and frozen at test time; no agent-written growing/episodic memory.
completeness_vs_topk_objective: Completeness-oriented multi-tool recovery within a top-k budget. The objective is to recover the complete minimal set of tools a query needs (queries require 1-5 tools), measured by Recall@K (K=3,5,7), not just a single best tool. It is framed against COLT's 'completeness-oriented tool retrieval' line; output is a fixed top-K list, so it is a top-k ranking objective aimed at completeness (recall of the full needed set) rather than precision-driven variable-size selection.
retrieval_unit: tool-API: a single tool/function entry (e.g. a RapidAPI endpoint, or a library function like numpy.argmax / pandas.read_csv / boto3 EC2 op). The retrievable unit is one tool, represented either by its usage-driven Tool2Vec embedding (averaged query embeddings) or as one class in a multi-label classifier head.
index_source: Static corpus, offline-induced. Tool2Vec embeddings are built offline by averaging the embeddings of training-set example queries associated with each tool; MLC and ToolRefiner are encoder classifiers fine-tuned offline per dataset subset. The index/models are frozen at inference; no online/test-time growth. Training labels (query->tools) come either from ToolBench or from LLM-synthesized ToolBank data.
index_structure_topology: Flat vector index for the first stage (cosine similarity over Tool2Vec embeddings), or equivalently a flat T-way classification head for MLC. The underlying ToolBench tool library is hierarchical (RapidAPI category->tool->API, reflected in the I1/I2/I3 splits), but Tool2Vec/ToolRefiner explicitly do NOT exploit or assume any tool hierarchy (a stated contrast with ToolRerank). So the method's own index is flat/non-hierarchical.
retriever_type: Hybrid two-stage: Stage 1 is a fast retriever that is either (a) dense embedding similarity over usage-driven Tool2Vec embeddings (E5 encoder), or (b) MLC - a learned multi-label classifier (fine-tuned DeBERTa-V3 base with an H x T head on the [CLS] token) that directly predicts tool labels from the query (a classification-as-retrieval / generative-classifier style). Stage 2 (ToolRefiner) is a learned cross-encoder-style reranker (fine-tuned DeBERTa-V3 xsmall) that jointly attends over the query plus the Tool2Vec embeddings of the Stage-1 candidates. So: dense + learned-classifier retriever, followed by a learned reranker.
retriever_learning_signal: Supervised, with multiple signals. (1) Tool2Vec needs no retriever training - it reuses an off-the-shelf embedding model (E5) and aggregates training-query embeddings per tool (usage-driven construction); the underlying embedding model is not fine-tuned in the main experiments. (2) MLC is trained with multi-label binary cross-entropy: label 1 for required tools, 0 otherwise, over the full tool set. (3) ToolRefiner is trained with per-tool binary cross-entropy on the candidate set (relevant vs not). Thus the learning signal is supervised similarity/relevance labels (query-tool co-occurrence), where the labels themselves can be LLM-synthesized (ToolBank). No RL, no LM-feedback loop, no interactive preference / Bradley-Terry signal.
query_construction: Raw user query is used directly as the key. For Tool2Vec, the query is embedded by E5 and compared (cosine) to tool embeddings. For MLC, the raw query tokens are fed to DeBERTa-V3 to produce per-tool logits. For ToolRefiner, the raw query is paired with the Tool2Vec embeddings of Stage-1 candidates. No query decomposition, intent extraction, or synthetic query expansion at retrieval time. (Note: LLM 'Query Polish' is applied only when generating the ToolBank training/eval data, not at retrieval time.)
query_granularity: task-level (one-shot at t=0): a single retrieval pass per user query produces the tool set; no per-step or trajectory-level re-querying.
when_to_retrieve: one-shot: retrieval is performed exactly once per query as a front-end stage (a fast first-stage retrieve followed by a single ToolRefiner refinement pass). The 'two-stage' / 'staged' / 'iteratively improves' phrasing refers to the retrieve-then-refine cascade, not to repeated test-time retrieval interleaved with reasoning.
retrieval_trigger_signal: Fixed schedule: both the Stage-1 retrieval and the Stage-2 ToolRefiner always run once per query. There is no uncertainty/confidence/agent-initiated trigger deciding whether to retrieve.
reranking: Yes - ToolRefiner is the reranking/refinement stage and is a central contribution. It is a learned classifier (fine-tuned DeBERTa-V3 xsmall) that takes the query and the Tool2Vec embeddings of the N Stage-1 candidates and, in a single forward pass, jointly classifies all candidates as relevant/not (binary cross-entropy per tool position). Explicitly likened to BERT passage reranking (Nogueira & Cho 2019), but contrasted with one-by-one cross-encoder rerankers: ToolRefiner reranks all candidates simultaneously, operates directly on precomputed Tool2Vec embeddings (not raw descriptions), and assumes no tool hierarchy (vs ToolRerank).
retrieved_context_refinement: rerank / refine via a second-stage learned classifier (ToolRefiner). Pipeline: fast Stage-1 retriever (Tool2Vec similarity or MLC) returns top-N candidates (N tuned over {8,16,32,64,128}); ToolRefiner then refines this candidate set by jointly re-scoring all N candidates and outputting the final top-K. No distractor-distillation/compression of tool documents; the refinement is candidate re-scoring/pruning. Choosing N is a trade-off: too few hurts recall, too many overwhelms ToolRefiner (peak at N=32 or 64).
how_retrieved_used: Retrieval-as-front-end for prompt augmentation: the final top-K retrieved tools are intended to be inserted (their descriptions/signatures) into the LLM's context for downstream function calling, reducing prompt length while preserving accuracy. The paper itself evaluates retrieval quality (Recall@K / nDCG@K) and does not run end-to-end LLM execution. ToolRefiner additionally injects Tool2Vec embeddings as inputs to its own classifier (latent tool representations used internally), but the consumer-facing output is the selected tool set for prompt construction.
planning_integration: retrieve-then-plan / plan-decoupled: tool retrieval is a standalone front-end that selects the tool set; any planning/acting by a downstream LLM happens separately and is out of scope of this paper. Within retrieval itself it is a retrieve-then-rerank (retrieve-then-refine) cascade. No interleaving with an agent planning loop, no MCTS/tree search.
reasoning_search_interleaving_granularit: per-query / per-answer: retrieval (and its two cascaded stages) runs once per user query, decoupled from any downstream per-CoT-step or per-tool-call reasoning. There is no per-step interleaving.
retrieved_item_representation: Two coexisting forms. Internally, tools are represented as Tool2Vec usage-driven dense embeddings (latent vectors = average of associated user-query embeddings), which ToolRefiner consumes directly. The consumer-facing retrieved items are tool/API entries (whose raw descriptions/signatures would be injected into the LLM prompt). No distilled strategy/guideline/workflow text is produced; the surface form is the tool identity (+ its description) plus, internally, a precomputed embedding.
abstraction_level_of_retrieved_unit: Concrete single tool/API (a procedural skill / executable function), not a distilled strategy, trajectory, or workflow. The key representational novelty is that the INDEXING signal is usage-driven (example queries) rather than the tool description, but the retrieved unit remains a concrete tool.
noise_robustness_mechanism: Two-stage retrieve-then-refine is itself the robustness mechanism: the more powerful ToolRefiner corrects Stage-1 errors and is shown to better separate tools with overlapping/similar functionality (reducing confusion among near-duplicate tools), yielding a more uniform per-tool failure distribution (mean 2.07 vs Tool2Vec's 7.86 mistakes per tool). Candidate-count N is tuned to avoid overwhelming ToolRefiner with distractors (too-large N degrades performance). Tool2Vec embeddings reduce the query-description semantic gap, lowering false matches. No explicit self-reflection / relevance-evaluator / distractor-aware adversarial training beyond the supervised classifier.
memory_type: none (no episodic/skill/workflow/graph/latent memory). The retrievable store is a static, offline-induced set of Tool2Vec embeddings / classifier weights over a fixed tool library.
write_back: No. The system does not write new experiences/cases/skills back into a store at deployment; Tool2Vec embeddings and the MLC/ToolRefiner models are fixed after offline training.
online_growth: No. The tool index (embeddings/classifier) is frozen after offline construction and does not grow at test time. (Adding a new tool would require recomputing its Tool2Vec embedding from associated queries and, for MLC/ToolRefiner, retraining or expanding the classification head.)
failure_experience_usage: No storage or retrieval of runtime failed experiences. Training uses positive (required) and negative (unused) tool labels per query as standard multi-label supervision, but these are training-time labels, not stored runtime failure cases retrieved later.
memory_evolution_update: N/A (no stored memory entries are mutated; the store is static after offline induction).
retrieval_as_learned_policy: Partially: retrieval/refinement is realized by LEARNED supervised models (MLC classifier, ToolRefiner reranker) trained on relevance labels, rather than purely fixed similarity top-k (which Tool2Vec alone is). However it is NOT a sequential RL/value-optimized policy (no M-MDP, no Q-learning, no reward optimization); it is supervised classification/ranking. So: learned models, not a learned sequential policy.
cross_agent_or_cross_framework_sharing: No. Single retrieval pipeline serving a single (hypothetical) downstream agent; no cross-agent or cross-framework memory/experience sharing.
benchmarks: (1) ToolBench (Qin et al. 2023/2024, ToolLLM; >16,000 RapidAPI APIs), split into I1, I2, I3 (increasing tool-hierarchy level / difficulty). (2) ToolBank - the paper's own LLM-synthesized datasets: NumpyBank (511 NumPy tools, ~20,000 queries), PandasBank (1,655 Pandas tools, ~70,000 queries), AWSBank/Boto3 (1,002 tools across EC2/RDS/IAM/S3/SNS, ~73,000 queries).
benchmark_family: tool retrieval (ToolBench family; plus the paper's new ToolBank: NumpyBank / PandasBank / AWSBank).
baselines: ToolBench Retriever (Qin et al. 2023/2024 ToolLLM dense retriever; reproduced from original codebase); COLT (Qu et al. 2024, completeness-oriented tool retrieval, Contriever-based; numbers taken from the COLT paper as code unavailable); and for ToolBank a Description-Based Retriever (E5-base fine-tuned on tool descriptions). Within the paper's own methods, Tool2Vec, MLC, ToolRefiner+Tool2Vec, ToolRefiner+MLC are compared against each other. ToolRerank is discussed as related work / conceptual contrast but is not run as a numeric baseline.
key_metrics: Recall@K (primary) for K=3,5,7; nDCG@K (K=3,5,7) reported as secondary (Appendix A.2). Plus diagnostic metrics: per-tool percentage failure rate (mean/std), and a GPT-4-turbo-judged query-quality win rate (60% win rate of ToolBank queries vs ToolBench queries). No end-to-end Pass Rate / Win Rate execution metric (retrieval-only evaluation).
headline_result: Up to 27.28 improvement in Recall@K on ToolBench and up to 30.5 (~30%) improvement in Recall@K on ToolBank vs description-based retrieval. Concretely, on ToolBench's hardest split I3, ToolRefiner+Tool2Vec reaches R@5=87.80 / R@7=89.70 vs the ToolBench Retriever's 63.88 / 73.73, and the abstract states 'over 25% higher recall' than ToolBench's retriever on the hardest split. ToolRefiner+MLC is generally the best (e.g. ToolBench I1 R@5=96.83, I2 R@5=87.92).
ablations: (1) Tool2Vec vs description embeddings for ToolRefiner inputs (Table A.1, ToolBench I3): ToolRefiner+Tool2Vec embeddings (R@3 80.58) > description embeddings with Tool2Vec retrieval (71.55) > description embeddings with description retrieval (66.00) - usage-driven embeddings clearly help. (2) Number of Stage-1 candidate tools N in {8,16,32,64,128} (Table A.2): recall improves then plateaus/declines; best N=32 or 64 (too-large N confuses ToolRefiner). (3) Embedding-model generality (Table A.3, ToolBench I3, no fine-tuning): Tool2Vec beats description-based retrieval for every model (E5-small/base/large, mxbai-embed-large, text-embedding-3-small), e.g. E5-small Tool2Vec R@3 63.12 vs Descriptions 20.62. (4) nDCG@K (Table A.4) shows the same ranking as Recall@K. (5) Failure analysis (Appendix B): ToolRefiner averages 2.07 mistakes/tool with uniform distribution vs Tool2Vec's 7.86 (skewed); ToolRefiner handles complex/long queries better, Tool2Vec struggles on simpler/shorter queries.
evaluation_decoupling: Yes (intrinsic-only). The work reports intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@K, nDCG@K) and explicitly does NOT measure end-to-end downstream task success; retrieval quality is fully decoupled from any execution outcome (execution is not run).
process_vs_outcome_metrics: Process/retrieval-quality metrics only. Evaluation scores the retrieval step (Recall@K, nDCG@K) and diagnostic process analyses (per-tool failure rate distribution, query-length vs failure correlation, query-quality win rate). No final task-outcome (e.g. tool-call success) metric is reported.
cost_efficiency_tradeoff: Efficiency is the core motivation. The two-stage design lets the expensive ToolRefiner operate only on N pruned candidates (not the whole library), and uses small encoders (E5-base; DeBERTa-V3 base for MLC, xsmall for ToolRefiner) instead of LLM-based retrievers; the paper argues LLM-based retrieval (e.g. AnyTool, iterative-feedback methods) adds latency 'up to several seconds'. ToolRefiner reranks all candidates in ONE forward pass (vs one-by-one cross-encoders like ToolRerank). The N-sweep (Table A.2) frames a recall-vs-latency trade-off (smaller N = faster but lower recall). No concrete wall-clock latency / FLOPs / dollar-cost numbers are reported.
context_budget_and_selection_count: Reported as Recall@K with fixed K in {3,5,7}; final output is a fixed top-K tool list (K up to 5 needed by any ToolBank query). Stage-1 candidate count N is reranked-then-truncated: N swept over {8,16,32,64,128} with best at 32 or 64, then ToolRefiner narrows to the final top-K. The motivation is to cap the LLM prompt's tool budget by retrieving few tools; no explicit token-budget number is given.
benchmark_construction_and_size: ToolBank (this paper's contribution) is LLM-synthesized: tools crawled from official API references (NumPy 511 tools, Pandas 1,655, Boto3/AWS 1,002 across EC2/RDS/IAM/S3/SNS). Generation samples T=10 tools and lets Llama-3-70B-Instruct pick M in [2,5] coherent tools (vs ToolBench's random co-occurrence), with 5 in-context examples; then a 'Query Polish' LLM step improves naturalness. Sizes: ~20,000 NumPy queries (19,530 tool combinations), ~70,000 Pandas (69,550 combos), ~73,000 AWS (70,816 combos). Quality validated by GPT-4-turbo judging (ToolBank queries achieve 60% win rate over ToolBench queries on naturalness/fluency/coherence). Train/val split 8:2; test set evaluated once.
builds_on: ToolBench / ToolLLM (Qin et al. 2024) for the benchmark, tool hierarchy and the dense ToolBench retriever baseline; COLT (Qu et al. 2024) as completeness-oriented baseline; E5 embeddings (Wang et al. 2022) for Tool2Vec; DeBERTa-V3 (He et al. 2023) for MLC and ToolRefiner; BERT passage reranking (Nogueira & Cho 2019; Yilmaz et al. 2019) as the conceptual basis for ToolRefiner; TinyAgent (Erdogan et al. 2024) and LLM2LLM (Lee et al. 2024) for LLM-driven synthetic tool-retrieval data; Llama-3-70B-Instruct for ToolBank generation; MT-Bench / LLM-as-judge (Zheng et al. 2024) for query-quality evaluation.
contrasts_with: Description-based dense tool retrieval (ToolBench retriever; EasyTool; ProTIP) which suffers a query-description semantic gap; LLM-as-retriever methods (AnyTool; iterative-feedback retrieval of Xu et al. 2024) which add seconds of latency and need iterative LLM calls; ToolkenGPT (learns tool tokens inside the LLM, needs LLM modification); fine-tuned function-calling LLMs that require frequent retraining; and especially ToolRerank (Zheng et al. 2024) - ToolRefiner differs by assuming NO tool hierarchy, reranking ALL candidates in one forward pass (not one-by-one), and operating on Tool2Vec usage embeddings rather than tool descriptions.
lineage: Group E (tool-use), tool-retrieval sub-lineage. Sits in the embedding-design / retrieve-then-rerank branch of tool retrieval: it reframes the indexing signal from tool descriptions to usage-driven query embeddings (Tool2Vec), adds a classification-as-retrieval first stage (MLC), and a single-pass learned reranker over latent tool embeddings (ToolRefiner). Advances ToolBench/COLT-style dense tool retrieval toward usage-grounded, completeness-oriented multi-tool retrieval, contemporaneous with and contrasted against ToolRerank.
cbr_cycle_coverage: N/A (not a case-based-reasoning method; no Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain case cycle).
explicit_cbr_grounding: False. The work is framed as tool retrieval / information retrieval (retrieve-then-rerank, multi-label classification, usage-driven embeddings) and does not invoke case-based reasoning or cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner.
tool_document_engineering: Usage-driven tool representation is the key lever: instead of embedding raw tool docstrings, Tool2Vec represents each tool by the AVERAGE embedding of example user queries that use it (closing the query-description semantic gap). MLC and ToolRefiner are trained directly on (query -> tool-label) supervision rather than on tool text. Description-based embeddings serve only as the contrasted baseline. So: usage/query-driven embeddings (a form of synthetic-query-augmented tool representation) rather than raw or summary-expanded docstrings.
index_content_separation: Yes (implicitly via the two-stage cascade). A lightweight first stage (fast Tool2Vec similarity or MLC) prunes the large tool space to N candidates, and only then is the heavier ToolRefiner applied to that small candidate set - separating cheap broad retrieval from expensive precise refinement. This is the retrieve-then-rerank progressive-narrowing pattern rather than an index-vs-on-demand-content progressive-disclosure scheme. [uncertain]
dynamic_index_and_protocol: Static index built offline; no live synchronization / CRUD auto-sync and no MCP/function-calling protocol integration described. The underlying tools derive from RapidAPI (ToolBench) and from crawled NumPy/Pandas/Boto3 API references (ToolBank), but the retrieval index (embeddings/classifier) is frozen after offline construction.
tool_dependency_awareness: Limited. The method does NOT model explicit inter-tool dependencies (output-of-A-feeds-B, shared auth, prerequisites) and explicitly assumes no tool hierarchy. ToolRefiner does capture inter-tool interactions implicitly by jointly attending over all candidate tool embeddings together with the query in one forward pass (so co-relevance among candidates is modeled), and ToolBank's generation encourages natural tool co-occurrence (M coherent tools whose outputs chain), but no explicit dependency graph or prerequisite modeling is used.
adaptation_mechanism: N/A (no case adaptation; retrieved tools are used as-is; refinement is candidate re-scoring, not adaptation of a retrieved solution).
